doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Wally Heider's recordings and the tapes kept at home
summary: He told Heider how he wanted the band balanced, kept the live tapes for 27 years, and refused to sell them cut up.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: tell you what I need now.” I’m the band leader, there was something I wanted to hear. You know, right or wrong, I wanted to hear something that I wanted. It started with, “You hear how the lead trumpet player, how you can hear him so well?” “Yeah.” I said, “Now let me hear the fourth trumpet player. All four trumpets. On the same level.” I wanted to hear the sound of a band, not protruding notes. Now great, now you hear? In the old days, by the way, it was hard to record the bass. All you heard was boom-boom- boom-boom-boom because everything was done almost on one track, or not even two tracks, just put into the thing. So I brought him a record of “Jack the Bear” by Duke Ellington, where you hear [scats]. I said that’s what I want to hear. I want to hear notes. Now the next thing, I don’t want to feel the drums, you put the drums up front. That’s the fire of the whole band. Put Mel Lewis up in front. We came in the next day and did that. We came in for a few days and did that. Perfect. By that time we moved to another club to record, and I had all these tapes in my house. And what it was, it was songs that we played before that we recorded before. 27 years I had those tapes in my house. Buddy Rich would come over and Shorty Rogers. And I had them on reel to reel. And they said, “Why don’t you put these out? It’s the greatest band in the world.” I said, “It’s only for you and I to listen to. Forget about it.” And then all of a sudden the band started to make noise. Rob McConnell, Bob Florence, Frank Capp— and I’m sitting with the greatest thing so I figured well — and also another thing it was the days of records and cassettes. And by the time we opened up our things, it would start out to be an ensemble band, of course after we opened it all up for solos I said the last four minutes was ensemble. We went home hollering, the whole band. Now the records and the tapes that Wally Heider recorded when we opened it up, they were like 15 minutes each, and records, you could only put about 20 minutes on each side. Now I didn’t want to cut them because it was some of the greatest soloists — so I wouldn’t do it. Then in 1986 Dick Bach, who owned Pacific Records, heard the records. First Gene Norman, do you know who Gene Norman is? He’s got a record label called Crescendo. The older Crescendo night club that I worked at with Woody Herman’s band, he heard them and he wanted to buy them all. But I said I’ll sell them to you if you put it out in a four package set without cutting them up. He said, “I can’t make any money there, Terry. I’ve got to chop this up so I can make a record out of it.” I said, “Forget about it.” Unless you buy all four as a package set — and he offered me a lot of money — and I passed. Then all these bands came out and Dick Bach came and said, “Terry” — and he’s a great editor — he said, “let me show you something.” And for example he took Opus Number 1, where there was a battle, it was about 15 minutes long, and about 9 minutes of it was Joe Maini and Charlie Kennedy, the two alto players, playing two choruses each, then one each, then sixteen bars each, eight bars each, four bars, two bars, one bar each.
